e.t: Abraham is the personal name of the man known throughout the Bible as Abraham. In the Greek New Testament, this word functions as a proper name rather than a general description or title. It identifies Abraham when he is named in genealogies, discussions of God's covenant, and statements about his descendants or faith. The name appears 73 times in 69 New Testament verses, showing that Abraham remains an important biblical reference in the New Testament. The word can also appear in a possessive expression meaning something belonging to Abraham.

Hades is the name of a realm associated with the dead. It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times and is consistently rendered “Hades.” The word appears in passages concerning death, the dead, judgment, and the future defeat of death, but its precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This word refers to an age or ages and can also express eternity. It describes time viewed as a period or lasting duration, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 122 times, showing that it is used broadly in statements about the present age, future ages, and enduring life or rule. Its exact force is determined by the surrounding words, but its central idea concerns an age, ages, or eternity.

This word describes being free from anxiety or without anxiety. It expresses a settled condition in which anxious concern is absent, rather than naming a particular action or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 2:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: not troubled by anxiety and able to be at peace. This is a descriptive word for a person’s emotional state or condition.

This word describes someone or something as “lawless” or “without law”—outside the rule or authority of law. It can characterize people, actions, or circumstances in the Greek New Testament, depending on the sentence. The word appears nine times across six verses, including passages in Luke, Acts, 1 Corinthians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, and 2 Peter. Its central idea is the absence of lawful restraint or conformity to law, while the surrounding verse determines how that idea is applied.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means to crowd up to someone or press against them. It describes people pressing closely against someone or crowding around them, rather than standing at a distance. As a verb, it portrays physical crowding or pressure from a gathered group. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 8:45, so its precise force there must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains direct: a person is being pressed by people who have gathered close.

e.t: This word means to deceive or mislead someone, causing that person to move away from what is true or reliable. It describes an active act of leading another person into error rather than merely being mistaken. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing a focused use for deliberate or effective deception. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but the central idea remains leading someone astray through false guidance or persuasion.

e.t: This word means “confirmed” or “to confirm”: to establish something as certain, reliable, or firmly supported. It can describe an action that verifies or strengthens a person, message, promise, or faith. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, showing a repeated emphasis on making something secure or dependable rather than leaving it uncertain. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “ox,” referring to the animal. It is a noun used to name an ox as a recognizable animal in New Testament Greek. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, across seven verses, including passages in Luke, John, 1 Corinthians, and 1 Timothy. Its meaning remains straightforward: an ox, without requiring a broader symbolic sense from the word itself.

This word refers to “fruit” or “offspring”—what is produced or brought forth. It can describe the produce of a plant, or people viewed as the offspring of a parent or group. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including uses rendered “fruit” and “offspring.” Its precise sense is determined by whether the surrounding passage speaks of something growing from the ground or people who have come from someone or something.

e.t: This word means to deter or hinder—to hold someone back or prevent an action. It describes an active barrier or resistance rather than simply a delay. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 3:14. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence depends on its context, but its basic sense is clear: stopping or discouraging someone from proceeding.

e.t: This word means “hardly” or “difficultly”: it describes something that happens with difficulty or is not easily possible. It adds the idea of difficulty to an action or statement rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Matthew 19:23, Mark 10:23, and Luke 18:24. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains that something is difficult or hard to accomplish.

This word means “knowledge”—awareness or understanding of something. In the New Testament, it describes knowledge as a recognized grasp of what is known, including knowledge connected with God, his will, and what people ought to understand. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense applies across several passages rather than belonging to one isolated setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “to testify that” or “to testify to”—to affirm or bear witness to something. It functions as a verb, describing the act of giving testimony or confirming a truth. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 5:12. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this entry explains the word’s ordinary meaning rather than the full force it carries in that specific verse. Its central idea is a spoken or written witness that supports the truth of what is being declared.

This word describes someone who is generous—ready to give freely rather than hold tightly to what they possess. It expresses an open-handed willingness to share with others. As an adjective, it describes a person’s character or conduct, especially in relation to giving. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:18; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force there.

In the Greek New Testament, this word means “leaven” or “yeast,” the substance associated with making dough rise. It is a concrete food-making term, and its exact force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words. The word occurs 13 times across 11 New Testament verses, from Matthew through Galatians. The supplied references show it appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, as well as later letters.

Jotham is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs twice, with both occurrences represented in Matthew 1:9. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader which person is being mentioned, rather than supplying a general word with a broad definition. The name is rendered “Jotham.”

This word refers to a reed or stick, and it can also describe a pen made from a reed. It names a simple, slender object rather than expressing an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times and is commonly rendered “reed,” while “pen” reflects its use as a writing instrument. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central sense remains a reed-like object used or handled in an ordinary physical way.

e.t: This word means “in vain” or “vainly.” It describes something done without a worthwhile result, or expressed in an empty, ineffective way. As an adverb, it tells how an action occurs rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 4:5. Its precise force in that verse must be understood from the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to shout.” It describes speaking or crying out with a strong, audible voice rather than speaking quietly. The word is used nine times in the Greek New Testament, across Matthew, Luke, John, and Acts. Its normal sense focuses on the act of calling out or raising one’s voice; the surrounding verse determines who is shouting, what is being said, and why. It can therefore describe either a spoken cry or a public exclamation.

e.t: This word means “to bless” or “to call blessed.” It describes speaking of someone as honored, favored, or worthy of blessing. In the Greek New Testament, it is a verb used when a person declares another to be blessed rather than merely describing a private feeling. It occurs twice in this corpus, in Luke 1:48 and James 5:11, showing its use in two distinct passages while retaining this central idea.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to meditate,” expressing focused or sustained thought. It can also mean “to plot,” referring to deliberate planning, especially when the thought is directed toward an intended action. Thus, the word describes more than a passing idea: it involves actively considering or working something out in the mind. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 4:25 and 1 Timothy 4:15. The surrounding context determines whether the emphasis is thoughtful reflection or purposeful plotting.

This word means “midnight,” the middle point of the night. It identifies a specific time rather than describing an action, person, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, in Mark, Luke, and Acts. Its uses include references to nighttime prayer, a nighttime request, and events occurring during the night, but the precise significance in each passage comes from its surrounding verse and context. The word itself simply marks the late-night hour.

This word means “yes” and expresses affirmation, agreement, or a positive answer. It is used as a brief confirming word in the Greek New Testament, much like saying that something is true or that an answer is affirmative. It occurs 33 times in 29 verses in the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what statement or question it confirms, but its central meaning remains a clear “yes.”

e.t: This word means “to overcome” or “to conquer”—to prevail over an opposing person, power, or difficulty. It is a verb describing victory rather than merely attempting or resisting. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to someone who conquers, has conquered, or will conquer. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 28 times, with especially frequent use in Revelation and 1 John. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence identifies as being overcome.

e.t: This word means to openly acknowledge, confess, or profess something. It describes a spoken declaration rather than a private thought, and it can refer to acknowledging a person, truth, or commitment. Depending on the sentence, it may also carry the sense of declaring, praising, or promising. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 26 times, commonly rendered “confess” or “profess.” Its central idea is making an open admission or affirmation with one’s words.

This word means “oldness” or “the old way,” referring to what belongs to an earlier condition or manner of life. It describes an established former state rather than something new. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 7:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to what is old in contrast with what is new. The recognized rendering is “oldness.”

e.t: It means to cover something, including covering a person’s eyes so that the person cannot see. The word can therefore describe physical covering or the act of blindfolding, depending on the sentence. It appears three times in the Greek New Testament, with English renderings for covering and blindfolding. Its central idea is placing something over or around another thing to conceal it or block sight. The surrounding verse determines which use is intended.

This Greek New Testament word means “many” or “much,” expressing a large number or quantity. It can describe people, things, or an amount, while the surrounding sentence determines whether “many” or “much” best fits. The word occurs 367 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 331 verses, so it is a broad and frequently used term for describing abundance or a considerable extent.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to hasten” or “to run up to.” It describes moving quickly toward someone or something, emphasizing prompt approach rather than simply being present. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in two passages in Mark and one in Acts. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a swift movement toward a person or place.

This word means “early” and can specifically refer to “early rain.” It describes something arriving at the beginning of a period or season, with the rain sense pointing to the first seasonal rains. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 5:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the early or first rain rather than rain in general.

“Root” refers literally to the part of a plant that lies in the ground and supports its growth. It may also describe an underlying source, origin, or firm basis when used figuratively. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs 17 times, appearing in both literal plant imagery and language about what lies beneath or gives support. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “to sift,” describing the action of separating or testing something by shaking it through a sieve. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 22:31. Its basic meaning is the careful testing or sorting implied by sifting; the surrounding verse determines how that action applies in context.

This word describes something that has been “eaten by worms,” or is worm-eaten. It functions as a descriptive word for a person or body affected in this way. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 12:23. The word itself gives a physical description, while the surrounding verse determines how that description functions in the passage. Its meaning is specific rather than broad: it points to being consumed or damaged by worms, not simply to ordinary sickness, decay, or death.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word describes bringing thoughts or people together—pondering something, conferring with others, meeting, or disputing, depending on the sentence. Its central idea is mental or personal engagement with something or someone, rather than detached observation. It occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and Acts. The word can therefore describe quiet reflection as well as an encounter or discussion involving more than one person.

This word means “to kill” or “to slaughter,” describing the taking of life, often with the forceful sense of killing an animal or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, especially in Revelation, where it is associated with the Lamb who was killed and with people who suffer death. It also describes Cain’s killing of Abel. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to firm confidence or to an underlying essence—the reality that gives something its substance. Its meaning therefore depends on how it functions in the sentence: it can describe a settled assurance, or what something truly is at its foundation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in 2 Corinthians and Hebrews. The glosses associated with it are “confidence,” “confidence/essence,” and “essence.”

“Friendship” describes the bond of affection or companionship between people. It points to a personal relationship rather than merely a brief meeting or general kindness. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in James 4:4, so its broader range of use within the New Testament cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is a relationship marked by friendship and personal attachment.
